claims.statement: With the same 109M encoder and corpus, a good-view text JEPA reaches the WIT alignment with DINOv2 (.109) after 21.6M samples that next-token prediction reaches (.111) after 900M samples, i.e. 42 times fewer samples.
claims.quote: Good views need 42 times fewer training samples than next-token prediction on the same corpus to reach the same alignment

control_usage.quote: the alignment that next-token prediction reaches after 900M samples

claims.notes: Method usage (21.6M samples) cannot be entered as an integer amount; only one next-token checkpoint (900M) was scored, so the 42x ratio is an upper value under the scored checkpoints, not a measured crossing point.

claims.statement: The PRH with JEPAs is no longer a hypothesis but a theorem (Theorem 1) and a tool, as demonstrated by real separately trained encoders (109M text JEPA vs frozen DINOv2) aligned without pairs.
claims.quote: This demonstrates that the PRH– with JEPAs–is no longer a hypothesis but a theorem and a tool.

hypotheses.quote: Our theorems are population statements over a finite world with injective renderings and matched marginals; real modalities are lossy
hypotheses.rationale: Known limitations paragraph (Sec. 7) states real modalities are lossy; Theorem 1 needs injective renderings.

hypotheses.quote: no experiment meets the hypotheses of Theorem 1 exactly, since our runs use LeJEPA and the image side mostly uses crops as positives
hypotheses.rationale: Sec. 7 caveat; Sec. 2.3 also says DINOv2 is a bad-view JEPA (crops), while the text JEPA uses caption views, so pi_1 != pi_2.

hypotheses.quote: Proposition 1 does not cover uniqueness under its full-distribution constraint, which we leave as an assumption
hypotheses.rationale: Experiments use LeJEPA/SIGReg; uniqueness up to rotation is openly assumed, not proved, for it.

hypotheses.quote: finite-sample training relies on the network’s inductive bias
hypotheses.rationale: Theorem is about population minimizers; trained networks are finite-sample; stated openly as a limitation, not checked.

claims.statement: Theorem 1: in the idealized finite-world model, if M>=2 modalities share one positive-pair distribution and the minimizers of L_pi are unique up to rotation, every modality's minimizer composed with its rendering equals Q_m h* for one world embedding h*, so any two modalities agree up to one rotation.
claims.quote: Let M ≥ 2 modalities share one positive-pair distribution, π1 = · · · = π M = π, and let the minimizers of Lπ be unique up to rotation. Then there is one embedding of the world h⋆ : Z → Rk such that every minimizer f m⋆ of Lm , for every modality m, satisfies f m⋆ ◦ gm = Qm h⋆ for some Qm ∈ O(k ), (2) so any two modalities agree up to the single rotation Qm Q⊤ m′ .

hypotheses.quote: modality m through an injective rendering x = gm (z), e.g., the pixels of a photograph or the tokens of a caption
hypotheses.rationale: Holds by construction of the idealized target (Sec. 2.1 setup); Lemma 1 (Sec. A.2) uses it.

hypotheses.quote: and rotating every embedding leaves Ω unchanged
hypotheses.rationale: Part of the definition of objective (1) in Sec. 2.1; the idealized target is defined with it.

hypotheses.quote: Let M ≥ 2 modalities share one positive-pair distribution, π1 = · · · = π M = π
hypotheses.rationale: Explicit premise of the theorem, declared in its statement.

hypotheses.quote: The key assumption is uniqueness up to rotation, which holds for JEPAs with second-order anticollapse under a spectral gap
hypotheses.rationale: Explicit premise of Theorem 1; Proposition 1 discharges it only for whitened MSE with mu_k > mu_{k+1}, not in general.
